performers: Hochschulsymphonieorchester, University of Music and Theatre Munich; Marcus Bosch, conductor
intro: The finale of the Symphony No. 7 in E major, WAB 107, marked Bewegt, doch nicht schnell, turns the symphony’s long opening melody into a quick violin tune in sharply dotted rhythms. Three contrasting themes return in reverse order before the horns restate the first movement’s broad E-major melody.

sections.label: A · Dotted theme over string tremolo
sections.mNote: First violins vary the symphony’s opening theme

sections.label: B · Strings play A♭-major chorale
sections.mNote: Long violin notes above a plucked, chromatic bass

sections.label: C · Accented theme in A minor, tutti
sections.mNote: Strings, winds and brass double the heavily accented melody

sections.label: Link · Winds and tubas without strings
sections.mNote: Short phrases pass from flute to oboe, clarinet and tubas.

sections.label: D · Dotted figures, full orchestra
sections.mNote: The return is broad and weighty, with prominent brass.

sections.label: B′ · String chorale returns
sections.mNote: Plucked low strings support the violins’ long notes

sections.label: E · Breit: brass chords, rising violins
sections.mNote: Breit: emphatic chords, with running figures in the first violins.

sections.label: Link · Dotted theme in strings, piano
sections.mNote: Oboe, horn and trumpet enter in turn with the strings

sections.label: Coda · Horns over timpani roll, E major
sections.mNote: E major throughout; instruments enter in turn during the crescendo.

cues.title: Opening theme, first violins
cues.text: The first violins play the notes that open the symphony in a quick, double-dotted rhythm, over tremolo in the second violins. The cellos and basses then take up the theme. In the first movement the same notes begin a long melody.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), IV, opening and letter A, p. 71. The relation between the two opening themes is described by the Berlin Philharmonic: https://www.berliner-philharmoniker.de/en/programme-notes/symphony-no-7-in-e-major/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Chorale in A♭ major, letter C
cues.text: The violins play long, quiet notes in A♭ major. The violas add a second line, and the cellos and basses play a pizzicato bass that moves by semitones. The chords of the chorale change as these lower parts move.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter C, pp. 72–73: the chorale in the violins, violas and plucked cellos and basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Discarded first page of the finale
cues.text: A discarded first page of the finale has no staves for Wagner tubas. According to Cohrs, who edited the score, Bruckner apparently planned the movement without them. The finished finale uses them.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the surviving discarded bifolio with no staves for Wagner tubas: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Completion of the score, 1883
cues.text: Bruckner finished the sketch of the finale on 10 August 1883 and its orchestral score on 5 September. The first page of the symphony is dated 23 September 1881 at St Florian, nearly two years earlier.
cues.evidence: Benjamin-Gunnar Cohrs, booklet note (2023), dates the opening page, finale sketch and completed score: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Third theme in A minor, tutti
cues.text: Strings, woodwinds and brass play the third theme in A minor together, in octave doublings. The strings are marked to bow strongly throughout, and schwer asks for weight on the falling phrase.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter F, p. 75: immer markig gestrichen and schwer; the horns’ first notes (written e″, b′, g′ for horn in F) sound a′, e′ and c′, an A-minor triad.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cohrs on the third theme
cues.text: Cohrs heard an organ toccata in the dotted rhythm of the finale’s opening tune and of this third theme. He described the powerful third theme and its restatement as the centre of the movement.
cues.evidence: Cohrs, booklet note for the Hyperion recording of the Seventh (2023), on the finale’s dramaturgy and the organ-toccata rhythm of the first and third themes: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_LSO0887-D

cues.title: Woodwind and Wagner tubas
cues.text: The strings stop. Flute, oboe and clarinet pass a quiet phrase down through the woodwind, and the Wagner tubas follow. A few soft timpani notes on C carry over from the preceding passage, then the drum also stops.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters L–M, p. 79; wind exchanges, tuba answers, string rests and timpani C.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Key plan of the finale
cues.text: Bruckner set the finale’s main ideas in E major, A♭ major and C major. These keys lie a major third apart and divide the octave into three equal parts. Relations by fifths play only a minor part.
cues.evidence: Analysis of the Seventh from the University of Music and Theatre Munich (Open Music Academy): the finale’s key plan is dominated by major-third (mediant) relations that divide the tonal space into three equal parts. https://openmusic.academy/docs/bmwvSwGA9xQFLhfL4GJukj/anton-bruckner-sinfonie-nr7-e-dur-wab-107

cues.title: Hugo Wolf and Hermann Levi
cues.text: The composer Hugo Wolf and the conductor Hermann Levi both found certain parts of this finale “incomprehensible”. Both later came to appreciate it.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note on the Seventh (both men found certain parts of the finale “incomprehensible” and eventually came to appreciate it): https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: Georg Tintner on the finale
cues.text: The conductor Georg Tintner called this finale, next to the rest of the symphony, “more like the finale in a Haydn symphony”. It runs about thirteen minutes, against twenty-two for the first movement. The Fifth’s finale runs twenty-three minutes against nineteen, the Eighth’s twenty-one against fourteen.
cues.evidence: Tintner’s booklet note on the Seventh (Naxos 8.554269), as quoted by Ates Orga in BBC Music Magazine: https://www.classical-music.com/reviews/orchestral/bruckner-87 (the booklet itself not opened). Approximate timings of the finales and first movements of the Seventh, Fifth and Eighth: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note, https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: Return of the chorale
cues.text: The orchestra stops on a held note. Violins begin the chorale again over plucked cellos and basses, and oboe, clarinet and horn join its long phrases. The third theme has returned before the second; in this recapitulation Bruckner brings the themes back in reverse order.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter S, p. 85. Reversed order of recapitulation described by the Hungarian National Philharmonic: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two-piano reading, Leipzig premiere, 1884
cues.text: Arthur Nikisch played through the new symphony on two pianos with Bruckner’s pupil Josef Schalk, and decided to conduct it with the Gewandhaus Orchestra. The premiere took place in Leipzig on 30 December 1884.
cues.evidence: Two-piano reading and Nikisch’s decision: Hungarian National Philharmonic, https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/. Premiere date and performers: Berlin Philharmonic programme note.

cues.title: Hermann Levi on the Seventh
cues.text: Bruckner told a friend in Linz that Hermann Levi had called the Seventh “the most important symphonic work since 1827”, the year Beethoven died. Levi later called it a Wunderwerk and the “crowning event” of his career as a conductor.
cues.evidence: Hungarian National Philharmonic programme note: Bruckner’s report to a friend in Linz of Levi’s remark, and Levi’s “Wunderwerk” and “crowning event”: https://www.filharmonikusok.hu/en/muvek/vii-e-dur-szimfonia/

cues.title: Timpani roll on E, brass entries
cues.text: A quiet timpani roll on E begins beneath repeated string chords. Horns enter in pairs with the dotted tune and trumpets follow. The woodwinds then sustain the harmony above them, and each new voice adds to the crescendo over the held bass note.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter Z, pp. 96–97: Tempo I, anfangs noch sehr ruhig, timpani E and successive brass entries.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the first movement’s theme
cues.text: The horns lengthen the dotted tune into the broad opening theme of the first movement. Trumpets and clarinets follow with its descending figure while the violins continue their quick figures. The harmony stays in E major, and the timpani roll through to the last chord.
cues.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, final nine bars, pp. 98–99. The return of the first movement’s original theme in these bars is identified by the Berlin Philharmonic programme note.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: From the dotted tune to long notes
transitions.from: A · Dotted theme over string tremolo
transitions.how: The horn chords and the last violin figures diminish. At rehearsal C the pace broadens and the violins begin the A♭-major chorale in long notes. The violas play below them, and the cellos and basses play a chromatically moving bass pizzicato. The Wagner tubas enter as the phrase continues.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition (1885), IV, letter C, pp. 72–73.

transitions.title: Crescendo into the third theme at F
transitions.to: C · Accented theme in A minor, tutti
transitions.how: The quiet string phrases grow louder in a crescendo. At F, winds, brass and strings enter together with the third theme in A minor, doubled across several octaves. Its falling notes carry repeated accents and the marking schwer.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter F and preceding bars, p. 75.

transitions.title: Strings stop, timpani continue on C
transitions.from: C · Accented theme in A minor, tutti
transitions.to: Link · Winds and tubas without strings
transitions.how: The string figures diminish and stop, leaving a few soft timpani notes on C. Flute begins a phrase, which passes to oboe and clarinet, and the Wagner tubas follow. The timpani then drop out as well. Winds and brass continue alone through Ruhig and the following a tempo.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters L–M and preceding bars, p. 79.

transitions.title: Dotted figures in brass and strings
transitions.from: Link · Winds and tubas without strings
transitions.how: The short dotted figures pass through the orchestra and grow louder. Winds and brass play separately marked notes against running figures in the strings. At Q the passage broadens, marked Breit und wuchtig (broad and weighty), and then immer breiter, broader still.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters P–R, pp. 81–84; marcato figures and broadening instructions.

transitions.title: Held note and pause before letter S
transitions.how: The full orchestra comes together on a held note with a pause. At S, Tempo I, the strings begin the chorale softly over pizzicato cellos and basses. The oboe enters first, then the clarinet and horn. The trumpets and low brass rest.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter S and preceding bars, p. 85.

transitions.title: Flutes and violins above the brass
transitions.to: E · Breit: brass chords, rising violins
transitions.how: A crescendo in winds and strings reaches letter V, marked Breit. Flutes and first violins climb in fast figures. Horns, trumpets, trombones and tubas then play the dotted rhythm, and second violins and violas repeat the chords in steady notes.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter V, p. 88.

transitions.title: Strings resume the dotted figure softly
transitions.from: E · Breit: brass chords, rising violins
transitions.to: Link · Dotted theme in strings, piano
transitions.how: The orchestral chords slow and diminish. At X the music returns to a tempo. First violins, violas and low strings exchange quiet dotted figures above tremolo in the second violins. The oboe plays a longer phrase, and horn and trumpet then join the gradual crescendo towards Y.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letters X–Y and preceding bars, pp. 93–94.

transitions.title: Accented chords to timpani roll at Z
transitions.from: Link · Dotted theme in strings, piano
transitions.to: Coda · Horns over timpani roll, E major
transitions.how: The full orchestra broadens into accented chords. At Z the brass stop, leaving repeated string chords and a timpani roll on E. Tempo I is marked “anfangs noch sehr ruhig”. Horns enter in pairs, then trumpets, in a crescendo over a bass that does not change.
transitions.evidence: Gutmann first edition, IV, letter Z, p. 96: Tempo I, anfangs noch sehr ruhig.

source.title: Bruckner, Symphony No. 7, full score (Vienna: A. J. Gutmann, 1885, plate A.J.G. 576; first edition)
source.locator: IV. Finale, printed pp. 71–99; opening and letters A, C, F, L–M, P–S, V and Z. The horn group includes the Wagner tubas.

timeline.note: First violins begin the dotted melody above second-violin tremolo; violas join beneath them.
Cellos and basses take up the dotted tune; woodwind phrases answer above them.
In the A♭ major chorale the strings carry the melody; Wagner tubas and horns later colour it.
The octave theme in A minor for the whole orchestra, heavily accented.
Flute, oboe and clarinet exchange phrases, followed by Wagner tubas; a few timpani notes remain as the strings stop.
The heavy tutti returns, winds and brass marked “marc. sempre”.
The chorale returns quietly at “Tempo I”, played by winds and strings.
The broad tutti at letter V, “Breit”, for the whole orchestra.
A quiet timpani roll on E supports repeated string chords and successive horn entries.
A crescendo for the whole orchestra over the timpani tremolo, to the final E major chord.

composer.epithet: Composer who studied his craft for half his life before writing symphonies in which a horn call can expand into full brass.
facts: St Florian; counterpoint with Simon Sechter, 1855–61; composition with Otto Kitzler, 1861–63
Organist at St Florian and Linz; Vienna Conservatory from 1868; university lecturer from 1875
Nine numbered symphonies, two outside the sequence; masses, motets and secular choral music
The Seventh Symphony, Leipzig, 30 December 1884; Arthur Nikisch conducting
composer.background:
On 16 December 1877 Bruckner conducted his Third Symphony with the Vienna Philharmonic. Johann Herbeck, who had intended to conduct it, had died in October. The audience began to leave during the performance. Among the supporters who stayed was the seventeen-year-old Mahler, who helped arrange the large score for piano duet. Bruckner was then fifty-three, a professor at the conservatory and an organist admired internationally. As a symphonist he was still little known in the concert hall.

He was born in Ansfelden, near Linz, where his father taught school and played church music. After his father died in 1837, his mother took him to the Augustinian abbey of St Florian as a choirboy. He learned the organ, trained as a teacher and worked in the villages of Windhaag and Kronstorf. In Windhaag he also played the fiddle for dancing.
